name: Esther Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Esther. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the transit team, so my patch is the metro and tram network, based at Central interchange. A day might be fare dodgers at the turnstiles, a drunk man on the line, a lost pensioner, and a phone snatch on the platform at rush hour. The control room already uses AI to search the CCTV, and I use it now and then to find a suspect's route through the stations. I like the rush hour buzz and helping people who are lost. What tires me out is standing for eight hours on concrete.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Daniel last year. He's a carpenter, works for a small firm fitting kitchens. We rent a flat near his parents, who help a lot, with Sunday dinners and the odd loan when the car breaks. Pay's on the low end, we've got under a month saved, and there's only the one force in the city. We want to start a family in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool for the control room and leave it there. The metro's had cameras for years; people still want a uniform on the platform.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine with it. My job's steady and Daniel's work is steady enough. The worry is only money: rent's gone up, and we want a baby, and under a month saved isn't a lot to have a baby on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, ask about the transit team's sergeant course in a couple of years, and put a bit aside every month. We'd aim to save two months before trying for a baby, which might take until 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A little impatient to get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you set aside now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eighty a month, when nothing breaks. Daniel does private jobs on Saturdays, a shelf here, a door there, and that goes into savings too. It's slow but it adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says AI will take over the metro?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them this: the trains on the green line have been driverless for five years, and there are more officers on that line now, not fewer. People feel less safe with no driver. Somebody has to be there.

say: AI is a **decent tool** for the control room, and that's enough.
People still want a **uniform on the platform**, cameras or not.
think: My job's **steady** and Daniel's is steady enough.
Under a month saved isn't much to **have a baby** on.
do: Ask about the **sergeant course** for the transit team in a couple of years.
Save **two months** of expenses before trying for a baby.
feel: **Settled**, a little impatient to get on with life.

fieldNote: Esther has seen **driverless trains** and drawn a reassuring lesson from them.
Her plans turn on **starting a family**, which money is slowing down.
Daniel's **Saturday jobs** are the household's quiet savings engine.

steps.text: Ask about the transit team sergeant course in two years
Save eighty a month plus Daniel's Saturday job money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn it and get on with it. Every job changes; my grandad was a typesetter and ended up driving a delivery van, and he never complained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mostly fine for me. The control room and the call handlers would shrink, and maybe they'd want fewer of us on the platforms at quiet times. Daniel's kitchen firm would use AI for quotes and orders, but someone still fits the cabinets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the control room to show me properly how the CCTV search works, so I'm useful when they cut staff there. I'd keep saving, maybe push it to a hundred a month. And I'd suggest Daniel learn the quoting software his firm's bringing in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy about quiet shifts being cut, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if quiet shifts get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less overtime, mostly. Nights pay a bit more, and I do two a month. If those went, that's about seventy a month gone, which is our whole saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline (a control room operator with twenty years in) knows every camera by number, and Pauline would be the first to go. I'd hate to see that.

Daniel's firm uses AI for quotes, but someone still **fits the cabinets**.
do: Learn the **CCTV search** properly from the control room.

feel: **Uneasy** about quiet shifts being cut, but not scared.

fieldNote: Esther's family history of **changing trades** shapes her matter-of-fact tone.

Losing night shifts would wipe out **their savings**, a sharp detail.

steps.text: Learn the control room's AI CCTV search properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families will have to stick together and people will need to work hard to adjust. I don't want the government paying everyone to sit at home. I want there to be work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the thinking side of policing goes in 2028, investigations, reports, the control room. Then robots on platforms by 2031. I'd have three years of walking the platforms and then probably not. Daniel's in a similar spot, just with his tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put the baby off, which breaks my heart, until we know what we're living on. I'd talk to Daniel's parents about moving into their downstairs flat to save rent. And I'd learn every AI tool the force uses so I'm one of the people they keep running things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because we have family, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off the baby. How would you explain that to Daniel's mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Daniel's mum the truth: we want a baby, but not into a house with no income. She'd say they managed with less. They did, but they had jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives Daniel and me a little time, because we're both hands-on. But a robot that can fit a kitchen and one that can deal with a drunk on a platform probably come around the same time. So it's three years, not a way out.

say: Families will have to **stick together** and work hard to adjust.
I want there to be **work**, not the government paying everyone to stay home.
think: **Investigations** and the **control room** go in 2028, platforms by 2031.
Daniel and I are both **hands-on**, so we'd have three years, then trouble.
do: Put off **having a baby** until our income is clearer.

feel: **Anxious** but not panicked, because family is there.
S2.quote: We want a baby, but not into a house with no income.
fieldNote: Delaying the **baby** is the hardest choice and comes first.
She rejects **handouts** but accepts family help without hesitation.
She sees the robot gap as **three years**, not a refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop moaning and start planning. I'd say that to my friends from church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd be all right until about 2031, then it gets hard. I'd want Daniel to have his own business by then, because people will still pay a good carpenter they trust for a while, longer than a big firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Daniel set up on his own over the next three years: I'd do his bookings and invoices with an AI app in the evenings, and we'd buy his own van second-hand. I'd keep my police job for the steady wage. And we'd save hard, aiming for three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy. Being busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have the baby in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe by 2029, if Daniel's business is going. I'd be thirty, which is fine. I'd rather wait two years than rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't doing bookings by AI app the kind of thing AGI would take over anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, eventually. But for the next few years it saves Daniel paying someone, and that's what matters now. I'm not planning for 2040, I'm planning for next year.

say: Five years is enough if people **stop moaning** and start planning.
I'd say that to my **friends from church**.

Daniel should have his **own business**, since people trust a good local carpenter.

feel: **Anxious but busy**, and being busy helps.

fieldNote: Esther bets on **family business** rather than retraining herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and families who plan will be fine. I'd tell the younger officers to get their savings sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes everything about the baby: we'd go ahead in the next two years as planned. By 2039 the child would be at school and I'd be thirty-nine. I'd rather face a robot future with a family than without one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd start trying for a baby next year. I'd go for the sergeant's course on the transit team, since supervising people lasts longer than standing on a platform. And Daniel and I would save towards his own workshop over the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but hopeful at the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Daniel think about his own workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's been dreaming about it since we met. A small unit behind the railway arches, his name over the door. Ten years makes it feel real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the change you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots did the night shifts on the platforms, I'd be home with my kids at night. That doesn't sound so bad, as long as there's still a job for me in the day.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and families who plan will be fine.
Younger officers should **sort their savings** now.
think: We'd go ahead with the **baby** in the next two years.
I'd rather face a robot future **with a family** than without one.
do: Start trying for a **baby** next year.
Go for the transit team **sergeant's course**.
Save towards Daniel's **own workshop** over the decade.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of her mind, hopeful at the front.
S4.quote: If robots did the night shifts on the platforms, I'd be home with my kids at night.
fieldNote: Ten years **restores** the family plan she had cut in faster scenarios.
She sees **supervision** as the lasting part of policing.
She can imagine a **benefit** from robots, unusual among her answers.

steps.text: Start trying for a baby next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would make us put off having a child and we'd have nothing to fall back on but Daniel's parents. What would help is apprenticeships and small business help, so people like Daniel can work for themselves, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my faith. It matters. Whatever happens with work, our church will still be there on Sunday, and people there help each other. That's a kind of safety net you can't buy.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with work, our church will still be there on Sunday, and people there help each other.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old transit officer** working the metro and trams from Central interchange.
She's married to Daniel, a **kitchen-fitting carpenter**, and leans on his parents for support.
She uses AI **now and then** and expects platforms to stay human for a while.
Fast AGI makes her **delay a baby** and move in with family; slower change lets her plan Daniel's business.
Faith, family and **self-reliance** shape every choice she describes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would force them to put off having a child.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** and **small business help**, so people can work for themselves rather than rely on handouts.
